headline: Advanced farm machinery and buildings ordinance revisions to Council for a public hearing.
summary: The committee reviewed proposed changes to the farm machinery and buildings ordinance, raising assessed value thresholds, and voted to send it to the Council for a public hearing. The committee also discussed the town's noise ordinance and zoning rules on sound analysis, including possible updates for low-frequency noise from data centers, but took no vote on that topic.
decisions: Advanced the proposed revisions to the Farm Machinery and Buildings ordinance to a Council agenda for a Public Hearing, with a unanimous vote.

Ordinance Committee September 1, 2026 Page 1 
 
TOWN OF WALLINGFORD, CONNECTICUT 
ORDINANCE COMMITTEE 
Robert F. Parisi Council Chambers 
45 South Main Street, Wallingford 
Tuesday, September 1, 2026 
6:30 pm 
 
 
RECORD OF VOTES AND MINUTES 
 
The Ordinance Committee Meeting on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, was called to order at 6:30 p.m. The 
Pledge of Allegiance was said.  Councilors in attendance were Autumn Allinson, Craig Fishbein, Thomas 
Laffin, Bryan Rivard, Christina Tatta (virtual), and Chairperson Jesse Reynolds. Also in attendance were 
Mayor Vincent Cervoni, Janis Small, Corporation Counsel, and Steven Allinson, Assistant Town 
Attorney. 
 
1. Call to Order 
2. Pledge of Allegiance 
3. Roll Call 
 
4. Discussion of Proposed Revisions to the Ordinance regarding Farm Machinery and Buildings  
 
Atty. Small explained that she cleaned up the language and outlined the changes that were proposed by 
the Town Planner.  The prior ordinance used an assessed value of $100,000 for farm machinery, and that 
has been changed to $250,000.  Farm Building assessments changed from a $100,000 assessed value to 
$500,000. 
 
Chairman Reynolds clarified that the state changed the way you can deduct, and in addition, our 
ordinance needed to be updated. Also, it’s a small number of people that this will affect. Atty. Small 
added that the Town can do more.  
 
Councilor Fishbein referred to Section C’s requirement that the building be actually and exclusively used 
for farming.  He asked about residential buildings on the farm. Atty. Small replied that this is from the 
State Statute and the house can’t be included.  It is per building. She noted that there are other programs 
for farmland.  Councilor Fishbein clarified that this is for the tax assessed value of buildings.  Atty. Small 
added that it is for buildings and machinery. 
 
 
Hearing no further discussion, Chairperson Reynolds asked for a motion to add this topic to a Council 
agenda for a Public Hearing. 
 
MOTION WAS MADE TO ADVANCE THIS ITEM TO A COUNCIL AGENDA. 
 
MADE BY:  FISHBEIN 
SECONDED BY:  LAFFIN 
 
VOTE: UNANIMOUS 
MOTION PASSED

5. Discussion of the Town of Wallingford’s Noise Ordinance and Zoning Regulations Relating to 
Sound Analysis 
 
Atty. Small explained that she had provided a copy of the Town of Berlin’s ordinance and the definition 
of sound and impact vibration.  If a data center meets the State qualifications, it would be required to have 
a host agreement with the Town, which can include sound requirements.  The Noise Ordinance itself is 
not really effective, and she hasn’t found a town with an effective ordinance.  The ordinance is enforced 
by the police, and testing requires special equipment and training. She suggested talking about what else 
we should be doing. 
 
Chairman Reynolds stated that he doesn’t want to demonize data centers, as we all use them.  The 
question is whether or not to include specifics on testing if we do a host agreement.  Atty. Small stated 
that we could add layers beyond the zoning level and would need to hire an expert.  Chairman Reynolds 
asked if zoning distinctions in the ordinance are appropriate.  Atty. Small replied that we can be stricter 
than the State. She suggested getting an expert to help with the definitions. Sound is complicated. 
 
Councilor Rivard asked if the ordinance or zoning regulations address the C bands.  Atty. Small replied 
that they refer to noise and vibrations.  Councilor Rivard suggested fixing the ordinance to make it more 
effective. He asked how to memorialize proactive measurement. The ordinance is silent on the C band of 
noise.  We should modernize the ordinance and cover all frequencies that are expected to occur and give a 
technical framework.  Atty. Small added that it may depend on the location of the facility. 
 
Councilor Fishbein noted that since the equipment isn’t used often, it may not be calibrated and the 
trained individual might not be available when needed.  We spent a lot of time on the ordinance, and it’s 
tighter than the State.  He added that the Council has the power to make the agreement with the Data 
Center.  He liked the idea of making it the responsibility of the Data Center to monitor and record sound. 
He agreed that it may be appropriate to add the C Band to the ordinance.   
 
Chairperson Reynolds stated that typically the noise complaints are about a hum that doesn’t go away. 
 
Atty. Small stated that she has looked at several other town ordinances and no one has taken it to that 
level.  She can ask the consultant we’ve used in the past if they’ve seen anything like that. She added that 
the ordinance hasn’t kept up with changes in zoning.  
 
Atty. Allinson added that the current regulations require the applicant to provide vibration and sound 
analysis by a professional and mentions low frequency.  It states that the operation shall continuously 
monitor and maintain records for 5 years and report to the Planning & Zoning Commission. This is only 
for the WI District, which is the only district that allows data centers.  That language can be expanded in 
the host agreement.  We should only expand the noise ordinance if we are looking at something else that 
would cause these low vibrations.  The zoning regulation and host agreement cover a lot.  
 
Chairman Reynolds agreed with looking at updating the ordinance. He asked what other things emit 
similar noises. 
 
Councilor Fishbein asked if we could get examples of what things sound like and how we can test for 
them. That way we know exactly what we are banning.  He suggested getting the expert involved again.  
He added that the ordinance draws a line for a border.  They cannot emanate noise past that border.  
 
Jack Arrigoni, 18 Martin Trail, reported that he has been investigating sound for the last two years.  There 
are different scales of decibels to be measured. The A scale is used in most ordinances and mirrors our

hearing.  Even if you don’t hear the sound, it is there.  He gave examples from other towns that identified 
low-frequency noise sources.  C and Z scales need to be added to the ordinance.  An expert can do a true 
sound study of all the scales. This doesn’t just apply to data centers.  This kind of noise is constant versus 
a motorcycle or truck.  If we have this on the books, we can measure if a problem arises.  We need to 
update the ordinance before any data centers are built. Stopping low-frequency noise is difficult. 
 
Councilor Fishbein asked if he is recommending adopting Berlin’s ordinance. Mr. Arrigoni said yes. 
Councilor Fishbein asked about enforcement. Mr. Arrigoni replied that it is a health issue. Atty. Small 
clarified that the police enforce the ordinance.  Councilor Fishbein agreed that we should explore 
updating the ordinance, but he is concerned with enforcement.   
 
Chairman Reynolds thanked Mr. Arrigoni for sharing his research.  
 
 
Hearing no further business, Chairman Reynolds declared the meeting adjourned at 7:20 pm. 
 
Respectfully submitted, 
Cheryl-Ann Tubby 
Recording Secretary
